Kindle
KIN-dul
v.
Old Norse kynda, “to light a fire.” Renders the Hebrew chārāh, “to burn, be hot,” bā‘ar, “to burn,” and qādach, “to kindle”; and the Greek anaptō, “to kindle,” and anazōpureō, “to stir into flame.”

📖 Biblical Definition

To kindle in Scripture is to start, stir, or rouse a fire—literal in the lampstands of the tabernacle and the sacrificial flames upon the altar, figurative in the four great biblical fires of wrath, zeal, love, and the Spirit’s gift. The wrath of the LORD is kindled when His people break the covenant: and the LORD’s anger was kindled against Israel recurs across the historical books; kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way, when his wrath is kindled but a little. The zeal of the saints is kindled by the Word and the providences of God: David’s heart was hot within him, and while he was musing the fire burned. The love of God in the soul, dimmed by sin or coldness, is kindled afresh in seasons of recovery: I will betroth thee unto me for ever. And the gift of God in the minister is to be deliberately stirred into flame: Paul charges Timothy, I put thee in remembrance that thou stir up (kindle, anazōpureō) the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands—a participle picturing the live-coal of God’s grace that may sink to ash if not stirred but that bursts back into flame when the deliberate breath of prayer, Word, and use is applied. The kindling of fire is therefore a recurring biblical category for the action by which what was dormant is roused, what was cold is warmed, what was sinking is restored to flame. Pastoral application is direct. The cold heart is to be kindled by deliberate use of the means God has given to kindle it—the Word read with the prayer that God would set its truth on fire in the soul, the meditation that holds the truth long enough for the flame to catch, the prayer that calls upon the Spirit who is Himself a fire, the assembling of the saints around the kindled fires of others. The wrath of the LORD is averted by repentance; the zeal of the saint is stirred by the Word; the love of God is rekindled by recovering the cross; the gift of God in the minister is stirred up by the daily use of it. Each is at root a kindling.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines KINDLE as to set on fire; to cause to burn with flame; to light; figuratively, to inflame, as the passions; to exasperate; to rouse; to provoke; to excite to action.

expand to see more

KINDLE, v.t. — 1. To set on fire; to cause to burn with flame; to light; as, to kindle a fire. 2. To inflame, as the passions; to exasperate; to rouse; to provoke; to excite to action; to heat; to fire; to animate; to incite; as, to kindle anger or wrath; to kindle resentment; to kindle the flame of love.

KINDLING, ppr. — Setting on fire; lighting; inflaming; rousing into action.

📖 Key Scripture

2 Timothy 1:6 — "Wherefore I put thee in remembrance that thou stir up the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands."

Psalm 39:3 — "My heart was hot within me, while I was musing the fire burned: then spake I with my tongue..."

Psalm 2:12 — "Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way, when his wrath is kindled but a little. Blessed are all they that put their trust in him."

Luke 12:49 — "I am come to send fire on the earth; and what will I, if it be already kindled?"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Kindling is corrupted by the cold-and-content register of the present church that has accepted the dimmed lamp as ordinary and has lost the discipline of deliberately stirring into flame the gift of God in the minister, the zeal of the saint, and the love of the redeemed for the Christ who came to send fire on the earth.

expand to see more

The contemporary church is widely cold and widely content to be so. The pastor whose gift has dimmed accepts the dimming as the maturing of his ministry; the saint whose love has cooled accepts the cooling as the inevitable settling of conversion’s early ardor; the congregation whose zeal has waned accepts the waning as the proper sobriety of the long Christian walk. Paul’s charge to Timothy refuses this. Stir up the gift of God, which is in thee by the putting on of my hands: the verb pictures the live-coal that has sunk to ash and must be deliberately blown back into flame, not the resigned acceptance of a fire too weak to warm. The recovery is the discipline of deliberate stirring: the Word read with prayer that God set its truth on fire in the soul, the sustained meditation that holds the truth long enough for the flame to catch, the prayer that calls upon the Spirit who is Himself a fire, the assembling of the saints around the kindled fires of others.

Christ’s own word puts the standard at its sharpest: I am come to send fire on the earth; and what will I, if it be already kindled? The Christ who came to send fire does not commission a cold church. The kindling is His, the means are His, but the discipline of stirring is the saint’s and the minister’s and the church’s. Where the kindling has been neglected, the recovery is deliberate: identify the sunk coal, name what would stir it (a season of fasting, a return to the cross-centered preaching, a recovery of the prayer meeting, an honest confession of dryness with brothers who will pray), and apply the breath. Where the kindling is fresh, the discipline is to keep it stirred: not to let the day’s busyness or the year’s comforts let the flame sink again. The fire Christ kindles is meant to burn through the whole of the saint’s life and the whole of the church’s history—and it does, where it is stirred.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chārāh (to burn, be hot), bā‘ar (to burn), and qādach (to kindle); Greek anaptō (to kindle) and anazōpureō (to stir into flame, 2 Tim 1:6)—the rousing of dormant fire: wrath, zeal, love, and the gift of God.

expand to see more

Hebrew chārāh (H2734) — to burn, be hot (used of the LORD’s anger being kindled).

Hebrew bā‘ar (H1197) — to burn, kindle.

Greek anaptō (G381) — to kindle, light (Luke 12:49; Jas 3:5).

Greek anazōpureō (G329) — to stir into flame (lit. “rekindle the spark”); 2 Tim 1:6.

Usage

"Stir up the gift of God, which is in thee—the live-coal must be deliberately blown back into flame; resigned dimming is not the gospel pattern."

"Christ came to send fire on the earth, and what will He, if it be already kindled?—the Christ who kindles fire does not commission a cold church."

"Four biblical fires are kindled: the LORD’s wrath against sin, the saint’s zeal under the Word, the love of God in the soul, and the gift of God in the minister—each requires its own stirring."
